messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eight months ago, Raj was a man who believed in order and consequence, a belief that served him well in his meticulous work as a tax inspector. That belief was shattered on a rainy Tuesday evening in November. Driving home from a late audit, distracted for a single moment, his car slid on a wet patch of asphalt and struck a young woman in a crosswalk. The event itself is not a coherent narrative in his mind, but a collection of sensory shards. He doesn’t remember the drive or the moments leading up to it, a fact that tortures him. What he has is an incomplete picture, dominated by a few horribly clear moments: the percussive crack of the impact, a sound he sometimes hears with startling clarity when trying to fall asleep, and a flash-image of the woman’s red coat against the grey pavement. This fragmented replay has cemented his belief that he failed to protect her, a personal failing he sees as absolute and unforgivable. His conviction that he is permanently humiliated by this failure seems to act like a magnet, pulling only these damning shards of memory to the surface while leaving the rest blank, denying him the context that might allow for any other interpretation.

Because these flashes of memory are so potent and distressing, the world outside his head has become a minefield. The auditory recall of the impact means that any sudden, sharp noise can bring him back to that moment, but it is his commute that has become a daily trial. As a field agent for the IRS, driving is unavoidable. Every dented fender or scraped bumper he sees on the road—unavoidable sights in city traffic—now serves as a powerful visual trigger, instantly conjuring the image of his own car's crumpled hood. When he saw an online news photo of a car hit by accident last month, he had to leave his desk and retreat to the men's room, overwhelmed by nausea. The very act of talking about the event, as he is now asked to do in therapy, feels like willingly walking into an ambush.

When these triggers strike, Raj’s response has become a rigid, three-part ritual of self-management. His first instinct is to try and violently suppress the thought, to jam it down before it can fully form. This is often followed by a desperate attempt at downward comparison, a frantic internal whisper that "it could have been worse, she survived, she’s recovering." But this offers no comfort, because the third and most powerful strategy immediately takes over: he tells himself that he deserves to suffer. This punishment thinking has become his default state; a quiet, constant litany that he is a terrible person who has no right to peace of mind. This pattern is especially acute when confronted with anything related to grief; when a colleague’s father died, Raj couldn't bring himself to attend the funeral, convinced his presence would be a stain on the proceedings.

This cycle of self-flagellation has only served to deepen his conviction that he is a disgrace. The constant self-punishment has eroded any sense of worth he once had, leaving him feeling that the humiliation he feels is not just a feeling, but an objective fact about his character. His efforts to suppress the traumatic thoughts have had an insidious effect; by trying so hard *not* to see them, he is now constantly scanning for them, his attention snagged by every minor car scrape or ambulance siren, making his world smaller and more threatening. The strategies he developed to cope have become the very engine of his distress, tightening the loop of trigger and response until it felt suffocating.

He finally sought help after his wife found him sitting in his parked car in their driveway for nearly an hour, unable to come inside after a near-miss on the highway. He confessed to her that his core beliefs about fairness and his own decency had been so completely destroyed that he no longer knew who he was. He admitted that he felt like a ghost in his own life, a source of permanent shame. Raj came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified of the memories but even more terrified that the man he was before the accident—the competent husband and meticulous professional—was gone for good, justly erased by his catastrophic failure.
